data.title: A hard landing could be triggered by aggressive rate hikes – BofA
data.description:
Bank of America analysts are warning that the Federal Reserve's aggressive rate tightening cycle risks triggering a hard landing for the economy, with GDP and earnings-per-share growth forecasts likely facing downward revisions.

In a soft-landing scenario, the S&P 500 (SP500) below 7,000 is an attractive buying opportunity, with market breadth improving by spring. If so, investors can position for a shift from rate hikes to cuts by moving into cyclical assets like crypto, chips, copper, consumer stocks, and real estate.

However, BofA analysts believe the likelihood of a hard landing remains underappreciated—they expect GDP and earnings-per-share forecasts to be revised downward and warned that the current AI-driven capital expenditure and wealth-driven “boom loop” could flip into a “doom loop” that forces investors to reduce stock allocations.

For now, with uncertainty elevated, investors are retreating to what they already own and clustering in low-volatility, defensive value positions as they wait to see which scenario unfolds.

BofA drew striking parallels to the 2000 tech bubble, noting that markets were trading in “bubble” territory back in May but are now trading "post-bubble."

During the 2000 bubble's aftermath, staples (XLP), utilities (XLU), and financials (XLF) were the biggest outperformers with returns between 45% and 60%, while tech (XLK) and telecoms (XTL) were the largest underperformers with returns around -50% and -40%.

The analysts warn that "Fed hikes led to recession and proper bear markets in 2001," and with voters demanding “affordability” through midterm elections, the March 18th or April 28th FOMC meetings represent the earliest points when investors can discount the tightening cycle ending.

The research identified two key economic drivers now under pressure: U.S. household equity wealth, which is down approximately $5T quarter-to-date though still up roughly $8T in 2026, and AI capital expenditure from hyperscalers forecasting $1.3T in spending despite negative free cash flow.

BofA noted that "voters, bond markets, asset allocators are all saying 'slow AI data center buildout,'" which threatens the growth narrative supporting current market valuations.

For recession signals, BofA analysts pointed to unemployment claims and credit spreads as "always best recession tells."

Specifically, claims exceeding 250,000 and investment-grade spreads surpassing 100 basis points would signal the “boom loop” has become a "doom loop," forcing asset allocators to cut stocks and increase allocations to bonds, China, the U.S. dollar, and assets negatively correlated with AI such as real estate—a strategy the analysts describe as "long condos, short chips."

data.title: Biggest stock movers Friday: ANT, INTU, ABVX, and more
data.description:
Stock futures were mixed on Friday as Anthropic's record-breaking IPO failed to ease broader valuation and rate-hike fears weighing on the AI trade. 

Here are some of Friday's biggest stock movers:

Biggest stock gainers

  • Gap (GAP) +17% - Shares rose after the retailer reported mixed Q3 results, with adjusted EPS of $0.82 beating the $0.78 consensus and comparable sales outperforming expectations at Old Navy and Gap, offsetting continued weakness at Athleta and Banana Republic. Comparable sales declined 15% at Athleta and 3% at Banana Republic, missing expectations for declines of 11% and growth of 2.45%, respectively. GAAP EPS increased 39% to $0.86, helped by IEEPA tariff refunds, which also supported operating margin expansion to 9.9% from a year earlier. However, Gap lowered its FY2026 outlook, now expecting adjusted EPS of $2.29–$2.34 vs. its prior $2.35–$2.45 range and the $2.40 consensus, while forecasting flat net sales of approximately $15.4B. The company also named Ashley Kechter, formerly global president of Vuori and Fabletics, as Athleta's new president and CEO, effective December 14.
  • Buckle (BKE) +6% - Shares rose after the apparel retailer reported Q3 GAAP EPS of $0.94, beating the consensus by $0.10, while revenue increased 2.6% Y/Y to $329.2M but missed estimates by $7.95M. Comparable store net sales edged up 0.6% Y/Y for the 13 weeks ended October 31, 2026, while online sales declined 1.4% to $52.2M from $53M a year earlier.

Biggest stock losers

  • Abivax (ABVX) -15% - Shares plunged, marking their steepest intraday decline since June 2, after short seller Scorpion Capital disclosed a short position in the biotech company in a post on X.
  • Anthropic (ANT) -11% - Shares fell for a second consecutive trading session as a broader market selloff and concerns over AI-sector valuations weighed on sentiment following the company’s record-setting IPO. The stock dropped to $91.25 in early trading, compared with Thursday’s close of $97.17, but remained above its $83 IPO price after jumping 17% in its debut. Anthropic’s $107.3B IPO attracted demand for seven times the shares on offer, with more than half of institutional investors reportedly receiving no allocation, underscoring the strong investor appetite behind its debut.
  • PHINIA (PHIN) -5% - Shares slipped after the company announced the appointment of Gordon Muir as senior vice president and CFO, effective January 1, 2027. Muir, who joined BorgWarner in 2007 and has served as PHINIA’s treasurer since its 2023 spin-off, will succeed Chris Gropp, who plans to retire on March 31, 2027. Gropp will serve as a special advisor during the transition period from January 1 through March 31, supporting the handover of responsibilities.
  • Intuit (INTU) -4% - Shares fell despite FQ1 results topping expectations, as the fintech lowered its full-year revenue outlook on weaker-than-expected Credit Karma growth and issued a softer-than-anticipated Q2 forecast. Non-GAAP EPS rose 56% Y/Y to $2.91, beating the $2.64 consensus, while revenue increased 12% to $4.4B, above the $4.31B estimate. However, Intuit cut its FY2027 revenue outlook from $23.28B–$23.51B previously to $23.08B–$23.37B, citing slower consumer demand and revised Credit Karma growth expectations of 3%–7%, down from 11%–13%, while maintaining its adjusted EPS outlook of $22.88–$23.12. Q2 revenue is forecast at $4.93B–$4.95B, below the $5.11B consensus, while adjusted EPS guidance of $3.17–$3.22 also fell short of the $3.73 estimate. Separately, Intuit agreed to sell Mailchimp to Bending Spoons for approximately $3.68B, comprising $3.31B in cash and $368M in stock, with the transaction expected to close in early 2027.

data.title: Klarna partners with Adyen on agentic AI checkout
data.description:
Klarna (KLAR) and Adyen (ADYEY) (ADYYF) said on Friday shoppers can now pay with Klarna when an AI agent checks out for them through Adyen's agentic suite. It's the first payment option beyond cards available in Adyen Agentic.

Up until now, most AI shopping agents complete purchases with a stored credit or debit card, which precludes flexible payment options that many shoppers choose at regular checkout.

Adyen Agentic and merchants that already offer Klarna through Adyen can switch it on with no new integration work, the companies said.

With Klarna (KLAR) as a payment method within Adyen (ADYEY) (ADYYF) Agentic, the agent shows shoppers the same Klarna options the merchant already offers, such as paying in full, in interest-free installments, or with financing. Shoppers review and confirm every purchase before it is completed.

Klarna (KLAR) stock slipped 2.3% in morning trading as PayPo, a Polish rival, prepares for a potential initial public offering in Warsaw. Adyeb (ADYEY) rose 0.6% in U.S. trading.

data.title: Tesla sees limited hedge fund activity in Q3
data.description:
Hedge fund interest in Tesla (TSLA) was relatively muted in Q3, except for Altimeter Capital, led by Brad Gerstner, which opened a new position of ~1.92M Tesla (TSLA) shares.

Viking Global, led by Andreas Halvorsen, raised its stake to 2.34M shares from 548K in the previous quarter, while D1 Capital Partners, led by Dan Sundheim, increased its holdings to 512K shares from 402K.

Soros Fund, associated with George Soros, maintained its position at ~87K shares. Corvex Management, led by Keith Meister, also kept its holding unchanged at around 3K shares.

No exits or reductions in Tesla (TSLA) stake was seen in Q3 despite a 15% drop in price during Q3. Likely factors causing a rout in share price were disappointing Q2 earnings in July, concerns over rising AI and robotics investment, regulatory scrutiny of vehicle safety, and weaker-than-expected delivery forecasts, particularly in China and the U.S., that added further pressure.

data.title: Alpha and Omega Semiconductor in focus as Roth starts with Neutral rating
data.description:
Alpha and Omega Semiconductor (AOSL) was in the spotlight on Friday as investment firm Roth started coverage with a Neutral rating and a $27 price target.

“AOSL designs and manufactures power MOSFETs, power [integrated circuits] and wide-bandgap devices, with its own Oregon fab, Shanghai assembly and test, and a 15.1% stake in a Chongqing joint venture (JV). F1Q27A confirmed the AI mix shift, but the shares have risen ~38% since the print to $25.53 (11/16/26 close), and our target implies ~6% upside,” Roth analyst Kyle Smith wrote in a note to clients. “We believe PC weakness and mid-20% gross margins justify a discounted multiple, and view the stock as fairly valued.”

Delving deeper, Smith said artificial intelligence and server applications have now become 20% of revenue, up from 5.5% just last year. However, PC weakness is likely to weigh on the company's overall results.

“Traditional PC revenue fell ~30% q/q in F1Q27A, steeper than the 9.1% q/q drop in industry units (IDC), as PC makers cut component orders after a first-half pull-in and memory costs pushed up PC prices,” Smith added. “Management expects further weakness in F2Q27E. We model traditional PC and other Computing down 48% y/y in FY27E to $137Mn, then holding at ~$30-35M per quarter, with no recovery.”

data.title: As manufacturing labor shortages persist, robots help fill the gap
data.description:
U.S. companies are installing more robots in their factories and warehouses to help offset rising costs and labor shortages.

North American companies ordered 10,989 robots valued at $723.5M in the third quarter, data from the Association for Advancing Automation (A3) showed. That's about 25% more than the year-ago period.

Several industries saw substantial increases in robot orders during Q3, from automotive and semiconductors to life sciences. 

"The broader mix points to a robotics market that is becoming increasingly diversified across industries and applications," said Alex Shikany, executive vice president at A3.

While the automotive sector has been deploying robots at a scale needed to justify their cost for years, technological advances are helping other industries catch up.

Sectors including logistics, agriculture, life sciences and electronics together account for more than half of North American robot orders, A3's Shikany told the Financial Times.

Robot deployment is expected to further ramp up across industries in the years ahead. "Structural demand drivers, including labor shortages, productivity requirements, and manufacturing investment, remain supportive," S&P Global noted.

Labor shortages have been a persistent challenge in the manufacturing sector. A 2024 study from the Manufacturing Institute and Deloitte projected that the U.S. manufacturing industry may need some 3.8M jobs to be filled within the next decade.

With manufacturers struggling to recruit and retain talent, robots can help fill the gap. Industrial robots are effective when it comes to grunt work, but they require costly and extensive programming to handle more complex processes.

"AI could ease these constraints through improved machine vision, automated programming, simulation, and motion planning," S&P stated.

Deploying robots can also be an effective counter to another worrying trend – declining birth rates.

Around 26% of the manufacturing workforce is aged 55 or older. Only 8% are aged 16 to 24, compared to about 13% in other sectors.

All these factors have led to companies accelerating automation, pushing robot density in the global manufacturing sector to a new peak.

Robot density is the number of operational industrial robots relative to the number of employees, as measured by the International Federation of Robotics. The global average baseline has risen to 152 units per 10,000 employees within five years (2020-2025).

South Korea is at the top of leaderboard, with 1,066 industrial units per 10,000 employees. Singapore is in second place with 873 units, while Germany is third, at 469 units.

Meanwhile, the U.S. is ranked 8th worldwide with 323 units per 10,000 employees. The U.S. also trails China in terms of manufacturing and deploying robots.

"We need to double, triple the amount of robotic automation within 5-8 years, or I believe we will lose a significant share of what remains of our manufacturing to China," Robert Atkinson, founder of the Information Technology and Innovation Foundation, told FT. "But we're nowhere near."

Notable robotics firms include Agility Robotics (AGLT), Hyundai (HYMLF)-owned Boston Dynamics, Tesla (TSLA), Figure AI, Apptronik, XPeng (XPEV), Unitree, Intuitive Surgical (ISRG), Symbotic (SYM), Teradyne (TER), Rockwell Automation (ROK), Cognex (CGNX), Serve Robotics (SERV), Ouster (OUST), Knightscope (KSCP) 

AI models and frameworks for robotics include Gemini Robotics and RT-2 from Google (GOOGL), Nvidia's (NVDA) GR00T and Hugging Face's LeRobot.

data.title: Wall Street trades mixed as the Dow rebounds but tech remains under pressure
data.description:
Wall Street’s major averages were mixed on Friday, as a further tech selloff has put the main indices on track for their steepest weekly declines in over a year, as fresh weakness in artificial intelligence stocks fueled wider market concerns.

The blue-chip Dow (DJI) was last +0.5%, the benchmark S&P 500 (SP500) was last -0.5%, and the tech-focused Nasdaq Composite (COMP:IND) was last -1.6%. 

From a sector-by-sector basis, eight of the 11 segments were in positive trading territory, with consumer staples leading the way higher, while info tech has been the weakest area. 

Sentiment toward artificial intelligence stocks remained under pressure after Anthropic's (ANT) much-anticipated public market debut failed to provide the boost investors had hoped for, extending a volatile week for equities. 

The latest declines followed a bruising Thursday session in which all three major indexes fell more than 2%, with the Dow closing below 50,000 for the first time since June. 

The U.S. 2-year Treasury yield (US2Y) dropped 9 basis points to 4.67%, the U.S. 10-year Treasury yield (US10Y) shifted down 8 basis points to 4.96%, and the U.S. 30-year Treasury yield (US30Y) moved down 5 basis points to 5.35%. 

As for other stocks that were on the move, shares of Fair Isaac Corp. (FICO) advanced +6.2%, while shares of Sandisk (SNDK) dropped -10.5%.
